analysis.one_liner: Exempts small businesses, homeowners, and nonprofits from Superfund cleanup liability for ordinary household waste.
analysis.headline: A single House Democrat introduced the bill in September 1999 with zero cosponsors; two committees referred it to subcommittees, no hearing or vote ever happened, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Superfund is the federal law that makes anyone connected to a contaminated site pay for cleaning it up — sometimes including small firms and homeowners who only sent ordinary trash to a landfill. This bill would have shielded businesses with 100 or fewer employees, small nonprofits, and residential property owners from that liability when their only connection was household garbage or sewage sludge. It would also have given buyers of potentially contaminated land clearer legal protection if they paid for a standard environmental site assessment, and would have shielded buyers who redevelop contaminated sites from owner liability, while giving the government a lien to recover cleanup costs from the land's increased value.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses (100 or fewer employees), small nonprofit organizations, and owners of residential property would be exempt from cleanup liability tied only to ordinary municipal trash or sewage sludge they sent for disposal [S3]. Buyers of property acquired after April 1994 would get a defined 'innocent landowner' defense if they had a standard environmental site assessment done [S3]. Bona fide buyers who redevelop contaminated sites would be shielded from owner-based cleanup liability if they disclosed hazards, took care of the site, and cooperated with cleanup crews [S3]. Environmental consulting firms would gain a legal market for the assessments the bill requires [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses, nonprofits, and land buyers

how_it_helps.text: A small business (100 or fewer employees), small nonprofit, or residential property owner would not be liable for Superfund cleanup costs when its only connection was arranging disposal or transport of ordinary municipal solid waste or sewage sludge, so long as it did not impede the cleanup [S3].

A buyer of property acquired after April 15, 1994 would be treated as having made 'all appropriate inquiry' into prior contamination — the key to an innocent landowner defense — if an environmental site assessment meeting an American Society for Testing and Materials standard was done within 180 days before purchase [S3].

Bona fide prospective purchasers of contaminated sites would be freed from liability based solely on owning or operating the facility, if they gave required notices, took reasonable steps against releases, and cooperated with response actions; the federal government would get a lien on the property for cleanup costs up to the increase in the land's fair market value [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The bill states it would have no effect on the liability of any other person, so large generators and waste companies would remain on the hook [S3]. But where exempted small parties would previously have contributed to cleanup costs, that money shifts to other responsible parties and, if they cannot pay, to the Superfund trust funded by taxpayers. Land buyers would bear the cost of the required environmental site assessments, and redevelopers could see part of their property's added value claimed by a federal windfall lien [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Other responsible parties and, ultimately, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Every dollar of cleanup contribution excused for small parties must come from somewhere: the bill leaves other liable parties fully responsible [S3], but if they are insolvent or unidentified, unrecovered costs fall on the Superfund trust, which is financed by taxpayers.

The innocent landowner defense applies only to property acquired after April 15, 1994, and requires a paid environmental site assessment meeting a specific ASTM standard — a real expense for a small buyer, and no relief at all for longtime owners of contaminated land [S3].

The windfall lien lets the government claim from a redeveloper's property up to the increase in fair market value attributable to a cleanup, which reduces the financial incentive to redevelop contaminated sites that the liability shield is meant to create [S3].
Narrowing who can be charged for cleanups, even at the margins, can reduce the total pot of money available to actually remediate sites where communities live.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is well targeted: it reaches only parties whose link to a site was ordinary household trash or sewage sludge, leaves larger polluters fully liable, and even recovers government costs through a lien. The main honest objection is cost-shifting — small parties stop paying, and someone else must — plus the assessment costs and liens imposed on buyers. Many of these same ideas (innocent landowner defenses and prospective purchaser protections) were later enacted in a 2002 brownfields law, suggesting Congress ultimately saw the approach as workable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees for the rest of the two-year Congress and was never heard, amended, or voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak (D-MI) introduced the bill on September 23, 1999; no other member cosponsored it [S1].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment on September 24, 1999, and to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials on November 1, 1999 [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: small businesses, small nonprofits, homeowners, and land buyers remained fully exposed to Superfund cleanup liability, and the EPA kept its existing broad authority to charge anyone connected to a contaminated site. The main beneficiaries of inaction were the government's cost-recovery position and any responsible parties who might otherwise have absorbed a larger share of cleanup costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA's existing cost-recovery power; no one else

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no member of either party cosponsored it, and the Republican-run committees took no action, so no vote ever revealed a partisan split.

industries.industry: Small businesses (100 or fewer employees) and small nonprofits
industries.note: These would be exempt from Superfund liability tied solely to sending ordinary household trash or sewage sludge for disposal, protecting family firms and community organizations from cleanup bills out of scale with their role. The exemption does not excuse parties who impede cleanups.

industries.industry: Real estate buyers, developers, and brownfields redevelopers
industries.note: Defined innocent landowner and bona fide prospective purchaser defenses would make buying and redeveloping potentially contaminated land far less risky, which can bring jobs and use back to blighted sites. Buyers would pay for mandatory site assessments, and redevelopers could see a federal windfall lien claim part of the cleanup-driven value gain.

The bill writes the ASTM Phase I environmental site assessment standard into law as the path to landowner liability protection, guaranteeing a market for commercial site assessments. The assessments also inform buyers about contamination, which serves the public.

industries.industry: Large hazardous waste generators and disposers
industries.note: The bill explicitly leaves the liability of any other person untouched [S3]. To the extent small parties stop contributing to cleanups, large responsible parties could bear a somewhat larger residual share.

Where exempted parties' contributions disappear and other responsible parties cannot pay, unrecovered cleanup costs fall on the public-funded Superfund trust. The windfall lien partially offsets this by recapturing value added to exempted owners' properties.
